49_marg3374: When Cyrus king of the Persians, Baltasar having been slain, had taken the kingdom of the Babylonians with Darius his uncle, king of the Medes, in the first year of his reign he sent back to Jerusalem about fifty thousand Jews, over whom he set Zorobabel and Jesus the son of Josedec, and commanded them to rebuild the temple of the Lord. They built the altar and laid the foundations of the temple. But meanwhile Cyrus died, and Artaxerxes, succeeding him, ordered the nations round about Jerusalem not to allow the temple to be rebuilt. So the work remained unfinished until the second year of Darius son of Hystaspes. In this year the prophets Aggeus and Zacharias, fearing neither the king’s edict nor the enmity of the surrounding peoples, exhorted Zorobabel and the people with him to rebuild the temple, because the time had now come in which Jeremias had prophesied that the temple was to be rebuilt. And Zorobabel and the people obeyed the prophets who exhorted them rather than the king or the peoples who forbade them.
49_marg3375: Darius is interpreted “generations”, and signifies a lover of intercourse and of fleshly begetting. Fittingly, then, this vision is seen by the people in the time of Darius, a people that, returned from captivity, had not yet built the temple nor had the glory of the former Jerusalem, but dwelt in hollow, low-lying houses. Rightly too is it seen in the second year, because two is an unclean number, which, first departing from the virginity of unity, is the beginning of all alternation. Whence in Genesis it is not said after the works of the second day were finished, as is added after the works of the other days: and God saw that it was good. The sixth month too is fitting, because this month has no solemnities of God, as the seventh has, but is like the six days in which the world was made, in which one labours and eats bread in the sweat of the brow. But because the altar had already been built, the word comes on one day, that the people, forsaking the shrine of Darius and the sixth month, may return to the unity of faith.

49_marg3411: Anagogically. The churchman who sacrifices the spotless lamb and has put on Christ ties holy flesh in his cloak when he sets out to instruct his hearers about the outward sacraments; and with this cloak he touches, by expounding, the divine scripture, which is bread that strengthens man’s heart, and is pottage, that is, a cooked dish, as are the apostolic feasts, which season and cook the flesh of the old law and offer it seasoned for eating; scripture is also wine that gladdens man’s heart, it is also oil that makes the face cheerful, it is also the food of milk by which little ones are nourished, and other such things. But while the hearers are taught through scripture about the outward sacraments, they do not eat it as sanctified food, because they are not refreshed within by the inner richness of the sacraments. On the other hand the author of perverse teaching makes unclean whomever he infects with his teaching. For the wicked too have bread in their teaching, but of mourning; and wine, but of mad drunkenness; and the oil of flattery; they have pottage too, when, to confirm their perversity, they mix in mystical things from the scriptures as a seasoning; they have other foods too, that is, various treatises, which, because they were written by the unclean and uttered by an unclean mouth, make whoever touches them unclean, and he will be led into their error.

49_marg3416: Allegorically. You who have believed in Jesus, consider the time when in your heathendom you served vices and did not build in yourselves the temple whose foundation is Christ, on whom let each one see how he builds. Consider what you suffered before, when you went to a heap of twenty bushels: whatever virtues and good works you seemed to have before Christ were, beyond your hope, unfruitful, so that it could be said to you: Have you suffered so many things in vain? And when you expected fifty vessels from the vineyard, a number made perfect when seven weeks are completed with the oneness of the Godhead, and thought you had the wine that gladdens man’s heart, the sacred number thirty was taken away, the age at which Christ was baptized and at which the priests approach the mystery of God, and twenty is left: the number Jacob, seeing it loved by Esau, sent him animals by, twenty and twenty. Though among unbelievers there is no fruit of good works for eternity, yet they are said to receive half the reward of their labour, when, hoping for twenty, they find ten, that is, fruit and glory in the present time for the labour spent; and this is so that they may not wholly despair, but, turned at some time, may lay stone upon stone; otherwise they will lose even the half. Whence there follows: I struck you with a blasting wind: whatever is struck by blasting wind and mildew and hail is reduced to dust and ashes, and nothing useful is found in it; and this because they do not return to God. But those who return will be blessed by the Lord. Whence there follows: from this day I will bless, and so on.

In the vine the Saviour is understood, in the fig the Holy Spirit, in the olive the person of the Father. As we read in the book of Judges, where the fruitless trees ask the vine and the fig and the olive to reign over them, but they refuse rule over the fruitless. So those trees come to the bramble, a thorny shrub, which hurts and wounds whatever it touches as if with hooks, and consumes its subjects with its fire, that is, the devil, who reigns in the barren. The Father and the Son and the Spirit reign there where the pomegranate is: a tree which, for its great multitude of seeds and its various cells divided by interwoven skins, yet all held in one rind, is always set in the holy scriptures for the person of the Church.
